speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the fact that Canadian beef producers are not allowed to use the food supplement DES while United States producers are permitted to use this food additive and ship such beef and cattle into Canada, what steps does the minister propose to take to effect a fair arrangement for Canadian cattle producers?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES CATTLE GIVEN DES-STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should clarify one thing. It is the male species of the animal to which you feed DES, not the female, and the banning of meat coming into Canada from the United States in cases where the cattle supposedly have been fed DES would not necessarily mean a total ban on the importation of meat. There are many things that have to be considered. We recognize that it is illegal to feed it to cattle and then to sell that meat in Canada. But we do not believe that any cattle that are being fed DES in the United States at the present time will be coming into Canada for several weeks because, as I said previously, no one is going to implant DES, or add it to the feed, and get any results from it until several weeks have passed. We are watching the situation closely. We are in consultation with my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We are in contact with people in the United States Department of Agriculture. I can say that a decision will be made concerning this matter before any of the animals being fed DES at the present time come to market in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I rose I was not aware that there had been some difficulty at the conclusion of yesterday's debate. If the fact I have been recognized has caused the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar any difficulty or inconvenience I apologize to him.
In entering the debate at this time I wish to join all of our colleagues who have extended their congratulations to His Excellency the Governor General and to his lady upon their appointment. As a couple they follow in the footsteps of many distinguished predecessors, and members of the House of Commons who know Their Excellencies know they have the qualities to carry out the job with dignity, warmth and very great charm. I also join with members of this House in extending congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) for their fine contribution to this debate.
I welcome the opportunity to enter the debate because it allows me to review, for the benefit of hon. members and for the benefit of the people of Canada, the progress that has been made in the solution of urban problems, especially the progress toward our goal as a government as well as a nation of making available good housing at reasonable cost to all Canadians wherever they live. Before beginning my remarks on housing and urban affairs more generally, I should like to devote if I may a few moments to matters that affect me as a minister from British Columbia which were mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. One of the highest priorities of people in British Columbia is the opening up of the northern part of the province and the development of their northern resources and northern industrial capability. The major port and railway program agreement made between British Columbia and the federal government announced the day before the Western Economic Opportunities Conference, will make those aspirations a reality. That agreement, coupled with a major further agreement to be signed between British Columbia and the government of Canada by my colleague and seat-mate, the minister responsible for regional economic expansion, will, as I say, allow those aspirations of British Columbians to become a reality.
A key transportation component announced at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference is the construction of the Clinton-Ashcroft link between the CNR and the British Columbia Railway. Although this construction is taking place in British Columbia, all western provinces will benefit from it. Those in this House who ask daily questions about the movement of wheat will realize that when bad weather closes the rail lines through the Fraser Canyon, the one outlet to the Port of Vancouver, as it has done on several occasions, the building of the Clinton-Ashcroft passage will enable us to keep the grain shipments and other freight moving between the prairies and the port of Vancouver to the markets of the world. Tnat, of course, must be proceeded with, as was outlined in that agreement, with haste.
I should like to dwell for a moment on recent federal contributions to western port development. Last year the federal government spent almost one half the total National Harbours Board budget in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am delighted to hear my colleague from the Progressive Conservative Party across the way say "shame" to that. That is usually the way they regard British Columbia problems.
Specific projects now under development include the $30 million Van term Container Facility and the $20 million Lynnterm Deep Sea Terminal. This kind of capital expenditure will be continuing for some years. Outside the Vancouver port area a feasibility study is presently being conducted into the next phase of the Roberts Bank port development. For Prince Rupert, the federal government, apart entirely from the railway expansion program, has already announced a $17 million program for port expansion. These are exciting and bold developments which will ensure a strong base from which to compete for world trade. Many of the complaints about our present system of administering ports cannot be measured in terms of personnel and money. The government and my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), the responsible minister, recognized this in the Speech from the Throne by calling for the development of a new ports policy aimed at establishing a high degree of local involvement.
I believe there is a pressing need, and I speak as a member from British Columbia, for an independent regional port authority for western Canada. For far too long we have tried unsuccessfully to evolve a single national ports policy for all of Canada. To continue to view all Canadian port facilities as a monolithic entity in the hope of finding a comprehensive ports policy is to miss entirely the crux of the complaints from the various regional ports, particularly those located in the west.
Vancouver and Prince Rupert are national ports, national in every sense of the word, but they are also western ports serving the four western provinces particularly, and the need for a national ports policy must therefore be reconciled with the essential requirement for greater regional involvement in their operation, their management and their planning. It is with that recognition that the statement in the Speech from the Throne appears in respect of the evolution of a new ports policy.

Our second main objective relates to the quality of life in the cities we have today, especially the quality of life in the central cores of our largest cities. I forecast that because of our transportation system, we will not have the ability to move all the grain for export this year that we could have marketed. The Western Producer reports that a string of 25 carloads of grain which had been sitting at Perdue since January 7 was finally picked up only a few days ago. The President of the National Farmers Union said the CPR cleared the Rosetown-Biggar line of cars on January 7, then abandoned it to the wind and snow, thus leaving it plugged and stranding any grain in elevators on the line. That is typical.
If I had time I could give instances of similar neglect throughout western Canada. Perhaps things are better in Eastern Canada. All this will cost us a great deal in terms of income, and I see no sign that conditions will improve. The minister has told us that more hopper cars will be provided. But the cars we already have are sitting empty. The railroads have simply failed to supply sufficient motive power. The minister responsible for the Wheat Board says he has met with representatives of the railroads and that they would not give him a commitment. Mr. Speaker, we own one of these railroads; the other is privately owned. Is the government so weak, so incompetent that it cannot extract a commitment as to what will be done?

I cannot see why we should buy it. It was given to the company in the first place and it has done nothing ever since except milk the public for everything it can get.
I turn, now, to another subject. To whose advantage will it be when the government finally gets feed grain on the open market? One of the sad things about this policy is that nobody will benefit except the traders in Winnipeg. The farmers in Quebec will find themselves at the mercy of the grain traders, at the mercy of the scalpers, with nobody standing in between. I have nothing but derision for the minister responsible for the Wheat Board and for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), if it comes, to that, when they say the Wheat Board will be charged with responsibility for seeing that the grain is in position after the commodity market is in charge of the buying and selling. Those two marketing arrangements are like fire and water; they just don't mix. How can there be a futures market which permits any corporation to purchase any amount of grain it wishes, and which is available for future trading, while at the same time it is someone else's responsible to deliver the grain which has been bought? The consequences of this policy will be an uneven flow of grain, whereas formerly there was even controlled flow. The Wheat Board cannot be made responsible for the delivery of grain which someone else owns.
One of the most rewarding discussions I heard last session took place in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Mr. Gibbings was appearing before the committee. One of the members from the maritimes said New Brunswick farmers were running short of feed grain. He asked the Wheat Board representative where the grain was, and was told it was in Thunder Bay. "Could I buy it?" the hon. member from the maritimes asked. The representative of the Wheat Board answered: "That depends upon who owns it". Of course, it does. That is the sort of situation we shall face after August 1.
I wish to say something, now, about the dairy industry. I wonder whether in the not-too-distant future the minister will be able to announce a policy enabling us to produce all the butter and the cheese we need. I notice a recent statement from Manitoba to the effect that the province is no longer able to produce all the butter it needs. I suspect the position is not much different in Saskatchewan. What incentives will be offered to encourage people to produce the butterfat and the butter we need, as well as all the other dairy products the nation requires. In at least one province powdered milk is being reconstituted so as to meet the demand for fluid milk. It is all very well for the minister to say that milking cows is a 365 days-a-year job. it is all very well for him to say we are now entering an era in which it is more difficult to keep people in the dairy industry. But it was the policies and actions of the Canadian Dairy Commission which forced or persuaded many small farmers to get out of the dairy business. They did get out, and the minister knows it will not be easy to bring them back. He says, and I use his words, that we shall have to re-arrange the dairy industry. Why did he not tell us what he or the government propose to do by way of re-arranging the dairy industry?
One of the most interesting meetings I attended during the last election took place in a little town in my constit-
March 6, 1974

uency. I happened to drive into the town at a time when a meeting of those interested in the dairy industry was being held. The town used to be a dairy production centre of some consequence. The meeting was attended by agricultural representatives as well as by officials from the senior levels of government. A discussion took place about the best way of persuading farmers to get back into the business of producing manufacturing milk, setting up tanks, transportation and so on. I listened to the discussion and listening, too, at the back of the hall, were women and men who had been milking cows only a few years earlier until they lost their quotas and their right to a subsidy was removed. I heard someone interject that this is not the case. But I read the letters and I listened to their complaints when all this took place. It will obviously be difficult, now, to get these people to go back. I say to the minister he had better take a hard look at the operations of some of the big monopolies and combines which are now engaged in this industry. In my opinion they are carrying too much clout and swinging too big a club, along with some monopolies in other lines of business as well.
The minister mentioned sugar in his speech and the fact that we have not done too well in supporting the sugar industry in underdeveloped countries, as was mentioned by the mover of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. He is right. We have not done very well in supporting the underdeveloped countries; indeed, we have done very badly. We should be supporting a sugar agreement and giving some support to countries in the Caribbean which need it, which have needed it in the past and will need it again. By doing this, we would also benefit our own consumers.

We are helping neither the disadvantaged people in the world nor the Canadian consumer. We can buy sugar in Regina cheaper from a company in Denver,
The Address-Mr. Gleave
Colorado than we can buy sugar from an Alberta company, and I can quote the figures if the minister wishes. This is the kind of food system we have in this country. It is about time we had a policy that benefitted both the consumer and the producer, and this is possible of achievement. But it is not possible through the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. It is not possible through the sugar combines that exist in Canada and which are presently under investigation. It is not possible with a 20 per cent increase in the cost of production faced by farmers in one year. Both fertilizers and machinery have risen in price.
Dealers in farm machinery in my constituency tell me that they cannot get an adequate supply of machines to run farms, and farming is a mechanized industry today. Neither can farmers in my constituency get a firm price for fertilizer at this point in time. I wrote the minister on February 11 asking him specifically what assurances he had been able to get from the fertilizer companies as to price and as to supply, and I have not yet had a reply.
I do not know whether the minister does not know the facts, or whether the facts are so horrible that he does not want to put them down on paper and admit to them. An hon. member to my right yesterday, I think it was, asked some questions about baling twine and did not receive a very good answer from the minister, who said we were short of sisal. We manufacture twine in this country out of material other than sisal. We also manufacture synthetic twine.
In this regard a pattern seems to be establishing itself. Things we need become in short supply; there does not seem to be any around. The next thing we know, the price moves up substantially. This pattern is becoming so commonplace that we really come to expect it. In the United States, the heads of the big oil companies were called before the responsible Congressional committee and charged with following the practice of creating a scarcity, then jacking up prices.
We would feel a lot better if we had some assurance from the minister that something really effective was being done to keep prices down. We have had no such assurance in regard to farm machinery, farm machinery repairs, fertilizers, and many other commodities that have increased costs for farmers. Neither do we have the assurance from the bakeries that the price of bread is not going to increase. The government subsidizes wheat for domestic use and we as farmers subsidize it also, yet the bakeries jack up the price of the bread and walk off with the profit. What a charade! What a joke! This is Liberalism at its best.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think I have made the most of the points that I wanted to make, but there is one further matter that I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister. I refer to the outbreak of brucellosis, which is a pretty serious matter. I thought the minister was most unfair when he was asked a question by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker)

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. Wagner
about this outbreak in his area. As a matter of fact the minister replied: "You guys better quit talking about it or else it's going to affect our sales".
I am very much concerned if that is the attitude of the minister, because we face a very serious situation as a result of this contagious abortion in livestock, or brucellosis, as it is known. It is proving very expensive to farmers. I do not think you can pay sufficient compensation to a farmer who has a good dairy herd wiped out by brucellosis; you just could not put up enough money. The same is true of a good beef herd. I would have been happier if, in response to that question, the minister had said he was carefully examining the department's procedures with a view to finding the most effective method of eliminating this disease, or else that new procedures were already in place. In my own area the farmers are greatly concerned about this question.
One last matter before closing, Mr. Speaker. In the absence of the minister to whom the Wheat Board is responsible, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture whether the Wheat Board would some day tell the House what its policy is toward working out a new international wheat agreement. Has the Wheat Board any plans to work out a new commodity agreement, and can it get the co-operation of the European Common Market countries, or Australia, Argentina and the United States, the principal signatories of the last one? Are they actively exploring the possibility? At some time I should like them to tell us if they are exploring the possibility of an agreement on sugar and other international commodities.
If we are to hope for or expect a stable return to farmers, there are two or three major things which must be done, as the minister knows. We must seek international commodity agreements. That is one thing. The other is that we must seek and encourage machinery throughout this nation that will give us stable prices and stable bargaining power for the farmer. That is the second thing we must have if we are to achieve the objective which the government has set. Frankly, I say to the minister, so far as this party is concerned, we will be judging the legislation which comes in not only by what it provides but by what it leaves out. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if there is stability of prices and income for the farmer as well as giving a fair break to the consumer, we will look at that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our tradition is such that in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, a member of Parliament is expected to pay tribute to His Excellency the Governor General, to the right hon. Prime Minister, to the Leader of the Official Opposition, to the Speaker of the House, to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply. Therefore, all these distinguished gentlemen may be assured of my most sincere regard, and I congratulate them for the work they have achieved in their respective function. I do not know any better way of giving them a proof of my solidarity than by anticipating their wishes and proceeding right now to the analysis of the outline of this government intentions that is called the Speech from the Throne.

I do not consider the official opposition's role as being the incense bearer of the government, praising it for its good deeds if any, sympathizing with its problems, excusing its weaknesses as if they were unavoidable. On the contrary, the opposition's role is to induce the government to do better when they only do well, and to condemn them when they do not properly fulfill the responsibilities that are bestowed upon them. Democracy is the better for it.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne leads us to ask ourselves questions, first on our real chances of success in the short and long term as regards the fight against inflation then on the suitability of the federal approach to urban problems, in the field of transportation or in other areas. In both cases, the very approach of the present Liberal government is controversial and debatable. Before explaining why and how, I would like to emphasize right away that the Speech from the Throne completely fails to mention the international policy of this government. Must we believe, Mr. Speaker, that rumours relating to the early resignation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), which have circulated for sometime, were or still are justified to the extent that he was unable to draft a few relevant sentences that could have given evidence of a new breath of the present government in foreign affairs? Who knows? It is strangely silent. One thing is sure, within roughly ten days at the most my party in keeping with the work it undertook to be better prepare to govern this country when the time comes will publish a work paper to make known to all both its orientation and its commitments with respect to foreign affairs. As many others that document will be submitted to our members for consideration and approval at our forthcoming national convention to be held in Ottawa on March 17, 18 and 19.
I further point out, Mr. Speaker, the remarkable discretion of the Speech from the Throne on the serious problem of regional disparity. I find but one sentence and even then a very short and most evasive sentence, and I quote:
The government attaches great importance to regional development.
And that is all. The need is barely felt to say that measures will be introduced to deal with transportation, freight rates and port facilities. Nothing is said about the need for an industrial strategy, an economic development strategy underlying the entire concept. Once again we have empty promises with respect to regional economic expansion.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) could speak at length on the expectations and disappointments of the people in his area and if necessary he could read to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) headlines on this subject published in La Tribune, a daily newspaper in the Quebec Eastern Townships.
Other areas in Quebec are growing impatient because this government is dragging its feet. The northwestern part represented by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) who, we are glad to see, is back among us today would even have more to say on this subject. Also in the same situation we find the Saguenay, Lake St. John and St. Muarice areas, where the working papers on regional development are more numerous than viable projects and where people are fed up with false hopes raised
March 6, 1974

in the Kruger manner; the Laurentians, where Mirabel is being built in spite of delays, makeshifts, if not injustices, when one considers the fate of expropriated individuals on behalf of whom I am requesting once again the setting up of a parliamentary committee; the North Shore that refuses to be merely an economic appendage of the United States; the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe Peninsula, where because of the failure in Cabano of a proposed community cardboard factory, the people are desperate and where the fishermen, according to the members for Matane and Gaspe (Messrs. De Bane and Cyr), are tired of being neglected; in the Bois-Franc area as elsewhere, bankruptcies have shown that the government economic growth policy is in no way based on a strategy of industrial and economic development; the Quebec area, where at times patronage and expedience have outweighed wisdom and long-term prospects and where, for example, Lauzon is still awaiting the government's decision about a merchant marine. This derides the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Comtois), but it does not amuse neither the people of Lauzon nor the unemployed workers; the greater Montreal area, where projects as tremendous as Mirabel or 1976 Olympics should not make us forget on the one hand the shocking and early disposition of farm lands in the area, and on the other, the pressing need, both for the people in greater Montreal and throughout Quebec, to see Montreal launched on a viable and sustained economic recovery likely to create permanent jobs; the Outaouais region nearby, which ought to be something more than merely across the river from Ottawa and which must not be taken away from Quebec heritage, culturally, socially and economically. Those Mr. Speaker, are the areas, where the citizens are living in the expectation of better days to come without uprooting themselves from their environment, days which would be planned right now in closer cooperation with the Quebec government.
In my own riding of Saint-Hyacinthe, several businessmen or contractors complain to me about the difficulties they meet with when trying to expand, to enlarge or improve their plant while some industries threaten to leave as did recently Crane Society Ltd., in Marieville. We are sick and tired of the same short sighted program, sick and tired of those piece meal loans without any planning. And failing recognition as a special area which I requested last year and for the reasons I gave at that time, Saint-Hyacinthe wants to know quickly and squarely what industries will the government encourage in the area. For instance we want to know when they will take concrete measures to establish an agricultural food industry in the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe. Those are the regions, the ridings in Quebec where the Liberals in the next election campaign will have to explain the silence of the Speech from the Throne concerning regional economic expansion.
In Quebec, we will force them to speak about regional economic expansion and unemployment because we have 250,000 unemployed in Quebec. Nearly 10 per cent of the labour force in Quebec is idle and the future is not very promising. We will force them also to talk in concrete and clear terms about the 9.3 per cent rise of the cost of living during the last 12 months. In the food sector alone, which is vital, there was a rise of 18.2 per cent during those last 12 months. Unfortunately, that is not the end of it.
The Address-Mr. Wagner
Let the Liberals come to Saint-Hyacinthe to Brome-Mis-sisquoi, to Joliette, whose distinguished representative has come back among us and who is certainly destined to assume great responsibilities in our team. Let them come to one of these constituencies or to any other.

speechtext:
They came and we saw the result. Let them come to our constituencies during the next election campaign and apologize to the people for their inertia before inflation and let them say that the main reason for the problem is the international inflationary spiral. [English]
There is quite a difference between a government's constitutional right to govern and its moral right to seek the confidence of the people. I doubt very much whether this government understands that difference or, even worse, cares about it. As long as the Liberal-NDP charade continues, as long as the pressures of big corporations and big unions frustrate both members of the coalition from acting on prices, wages and profits, this daily erosion of our system's credibility will be massive, and rightly so. No wonder people are losing faith. Gentlemen on the other side should not wonder why the young are cynical and the aged are bitter. We have no government.
Ministers are racing around the country eradicating what confidence might still remain out there. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is keeping a low profile for reasons that friends of the heir apparent know too well. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) leaves hints that he might like a switch of task, or something even more restful, and the consensus of Eglington, from what I gathered on my last visit there, is that he will soon have what his heart desires. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) snatches insincere-ties from the jaws of truth whenever he rises to answer a question. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) talks about football while inflation attacks the rights of Canadians to decent nutrition. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) is out trying to sell what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) is trying to buy back. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) wants to investigate in private what is going awry very seriously in public, and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) says: Spend, spend, spend a little more. What is $3 billion and some, asks he. As the Minister of External Affairs would say, that is the Liberal way.
They remind me of a company on the verge of bankruptcy, unafraid to amass as many creditors as possible. It would be funny if it were not so sad. The creditors are the Canadian people. The government is piling up massive debt, debt that in terms of eroded confidence, mistrust, cynicism and despair may carry with it a rate of interest our nation is unable to pay. Politics, if they are to have any meaning today, must be synonymous with honesty, integrity, and responsive government. Members of the NDP used to care about this. Indeed, they used to be the purists about our system and its accountability. In all sincerity I ask my colleagues to the left: where is this purism now?

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. Wagner

Where is the decency and the implicit humanity of Mr. Tommy Douglas' new Jerusalem? What, if anything, I ask them, have you said you cannot suffer as social democrats from this government? I have to wonder. I have to wonder about the young people attached to all the political parties, in the schools, and across the young work force. What are they to learn from this parliament? What are they to learn from this government? So far, they have learned that no Conservative policy is too repugnant for the Liberals to steal, no socialist principle is too sacred to be sold, and no Liberal policy is so solid as to stand on its own merits.
As a famous Liberal was wont to end his speeches-I am sure hon. members across the aisle have often heard this- he would end by saying, "Gentlemen, these are our principles-and if you don't like them, we have others". I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if that is the type of game we want to play with social justice in Canada. I wonder if we have the right to play that game with our nation's fiscal and economic policies.
Beyond this chamber, beyond the pundits and the trained observers in the Press Gallery, there are 22 million Canadians who, for the most part, are partisans of no political party. They are partisans of this institution we call democracy. They are poll workers in their everyday jobs, if you like, for the concept which we call Canada. They believe that this concept means more than politics. They believe it means justice, equity, unity and direction, and when we play with this concept we are playing with the faith and trust of those who make this country live and grow and prosper.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
When we attack their faith, undermine their hope, limit their fair share, we are attacking this nation's future. I would think that no member of this House would want to be a party to that.

Mr. Speaker, in addition to refusing to speak on many important issues, the present government, is at fault in its very orientation. While the government seems winded, without either imagination or daring on the international level, the same holds true on the domestic scene.
Inflation and the record of the relations between Ottawa and the provincial governments-particularly Quebec's- give ample proof of this fact. This country no longer needs intellectuals who are either bored or weakened by power, a power which they are gradually losing; this country needs qualified administrators who are capable of innovation.

Mr. Speaker, it is not true that we have to submit to the increasing inflation-any pressures and it is no longer true that the Quebecers' only real choice of a government is the Liberal party.
For instance, the cost of single-family dwellings built for the average wage earner went from $22,500 in October 1973 to $28,600 in February 1974. This happened at Laval, on the south shore of Montreal and elsewhere. It is not true that this is solely the result of international inflation.
When the owners or managers of well-known grocery stores have reached the point where, to operate according to the good old principle "the most for the least", they keep their employees regularly for two and one-half days every week, and week after week, only to mark up food stuff, it is not true that this is the result solely of the international inflation.
When some of those same merchants, these are facts, Mr. Speaker, and this happened in Montreal early this week, increase by one cent or more the price of some 400 different articles, it is not true that this is the result solely of the international inflation. When the large chain stores such as Loblaw's, Dominion Stores Ltd., Steinberg, Provi-go, Becker Milk and Harvey's Food, as well as several others manage to increase their profits from 1971 to 1972 respectively by 43.2, 188.2, 58.2, 29.4, 63, 646.5 and 78.9 per cent, and when we know that those same stores and others made even higher profits in 1972 and 1973, it is not automatically true that this is simply the result of international inflation.
When businessmen, the "big shots" especially, build up stocks like never before, whether it consist of heating fuel or mostly food products, in such quantities that they have to rent additional storage space to better plan their spiralling profits, it is not true that the only influence is that of international inflationary pressures. The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) and many others should try to find a single unoccupied storeroom in good condition in Montreal at the present time!
Mr. Speaker, the cost of living, especially as concerns food products, is increasing at a scandalous rate.
The poorest among our fellow citizens, and even those whom we say belong to the middle class, all the wage earners who-and I was happy to hear the prime minister himself say it-are not responsible for the present increase in the cost of living, want us to control inflation.
In my constituency of Saint-Hyacinthe as elsewhere in Canada, the government is expected to take immediate, strict, firm and energetic action tackling at short term both with the present effects of inflation and its causes at least its Canadian causes.
The present inertia of this government which, in the short term at least, is forsaking the consumer threatened by inflation, is already appearing as the basic cause of its impending defeat and proves to be, which is more serious, an accomplice of the worst injustice.
This government has in fact surrendered to inflation. Public opinion exacerbated by the "big one" annihilating the "small one" should compel this government to resign
March 6, 1974

and give way to a serious team ready to administer the country.
If the farm producer, his problems and his needs are finally better understood, so much the better, and with my constituents of Saint-Hyacinthe, I am the first to rejoice about it. But. .. beware, I want to enter the following caveat: If it is high time and commendable that politics serve the farmer a little better, let no one use the farmer to play politics, as has been the case far too long in Quebec politics.
Our farmers are also, and first of all, first class citizens and in this capacity also, they consume a great deal of products. On the farm itself, they know what their raw materials cost-always more. If they want more assistance, and rightly so, they do not want and do not accept, as several of them told me recently in my riding, to be used as short term "surety" by a government that has become helpless in the face of inflation.
On another level, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government has got us used to a strategy of clashes that provincial governments, including the Quebec government, and Canadians as a whole cannot put up with any longer. Measures to initiate a food production or urban transportation policy must not once more bring about a deterioration of federal-provincial relations here, must not either be brought to a term without any previous serious consultation to such an extent as to create new crises that almost invariably the present central government uses in order to appropriate jurisdictions which are not devolved to it.
We can rightly fear the worst here, especially when one reads in the speech, and I quote:
The Government will wish to consult with provincial governments-
-How cynical! What a return to the former arrogance which has already been decried, judged and condemned in October 1972.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks, because I see that you are making signs to me and because I hear my friends opposite say that my time has elapsed. I know that they have had just enough of it and that their conscience is bothering them. Duly so, and they will have a hard time trying to explain to the Quebec people the failure of the government. I conclude, therefore, by saying that this government, lacking in leadership, increasingly less recognized and accepted as a true, reliable and honest interlocutor by a number of provincial governments, less and less accepted as a conciliatory agent by an increasing number of Canadians, should retire from the bargaining table and turn over the direction of this country to a Progressive Conservative team, ready to take over, as a responsible alternative, and to a leader whose patience, persistence, determination, will and competence are more and more appreciated by the Canadian public as a whole and especially-a very encouraging and revealing sign-by Quebecers themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments regarding some aspects of our economy which is of interest to me as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and as a member for Levis.
As hon. members know one of the main objectives of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is to ensure
The Address-Mr. R. Guay
the adequate and constant development of production as well as of trade in Canadian goods and services by creating, for instance, a proper national and international setting, by encouraging production of new goods and services and the introduction of new production techniques conforming to the requirements of a developing market, by improving the use of resources and by seeking to increase the necessary outlets for our economy.
True to its objectives, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was deeply involved in the creation by the government of the Industrial Development Bank and the Development Agency for Small Business of which the Industrial Development Bank is the spine and the heart. Through this organization, the government is more than ever in a position to encourage small business activity in Canada, which are so essential to our economy. It often is the most effective means of producing goods and services which can meet the specific needs of Canada and it has the flexibility to cope with the production and local distribution requirements of the various regions of this country.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who has just concluded his speech, that these are positive measures taken by this government to help small and medium enterprises in the province as in all other provinces of our country.
An independent organization, the IBDA offers small and medium enterprises a highly diversified assistance, acts as local information centre for all government programs and services available to small enterprises, and it supplies the required information on the availability of private sources of financing, and even providing the financing in case of need. It assumes the practical responsibility for the advisory and administrative services to small business, including the CASE consulting program; the main responsibility for the development and management of the federal administration training programs for small businesses, keeps an up to date list of the various assistance programs offered by the government and the private sector; it cooperates closely with the federal and provincial departments and agencies as well as with the private institutions.
The wellbeing of our economy in the years ahead will depend on it. In brief, the IBDA plays an absolutely essential role with the small businesses on which it depends to a large extent.
As regards the textile industry, Mr. Speaker, small business-and I think this is closely related to the riding of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe which contains several textile firms-in its multiple aspects is of vital importance to this country.
Despite a manpower shortage and the problems it is facing today to get supplies of natural and synthetic fibers, the Canadian textile industry usually maintains its operations at the high level that was observed during 1973 when substantial increases in sales and profits were recorded.
Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce officials have done their best to help this industry get supplies of petrochemical products and it is expected that this spring

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. R. Guay
the situation will improve a little in this area. The petrochemical product shortage is now felt on a worldwide basis, but I am pleased to see that Canadian producers enjoy a very favourable position as compared with most of their foreign competitors.
The Canadian capacity to produce synthetic fibres is now expanding, particularly in acrylics, nylon and polyesters. You know that Du Pont of Canada Limited announced that it plans to build a $40 million polyester plant in Coteau-du-Lac, in the province of Quebec, with production slated for 1976. Therefore, I think that the outlook for our textile industry is promising and I am pleased about it.
Mr. Speaker, our shipyards are an example of the prosperity of the Canadian industry, encouraged by government measures. Despite a shortage of steel and delays in the delivery of diesel engines, our shipyards are now operating at full capacity. Shipyards throughout Canada, and particularly in Lauzon, still benefit from STAP, the Shipbuilding Temporary Assistance Program of the Department of Industry, Trade, and Commerce which has been extended. This program implemented on November 27, 1970, provides grants to the builders of ships which will be registered in foreign countries. The maximum grant is 17 per cent of the certified cost of the ship, with restrictions relating to the Canadian content and the minimum size of ships. The extension of this program will make it possible to pay subsidies for ships completed before October 31, 1978 and ordered before March 31, 1975. This Canadian industry thus contributes to the overall prosperity of our country and is a good example of Canadian technology competing with that of big industrialized countries.
It is well known that this matter is of special interest to me, since there is a very important shipyard in my riding of Levis. The level of employment in Quebec shipyards is relatively high at present and it seems this situation will last until 1976. We are very happy about it. This high level of employment is due to contracts secured thanks to STAP adopted by the Canadian government in 1971. However, we are concerned about what will happen to employment after 1976 and about the long term future of that industry because studies now being made in various quarters seem to be unanimous in their fear of an overcapacity to produce in the years prior to 1980. That is why we believe that foresight is necessary on the part of the government in this area and a long term policy must immediatly be set up.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe is nodding his head and I am glad about it but I find it completely abnormal coming from that hon. member. Newspapermen in the press gallery might say that I am criticizing this government. No. On this side of the House we want to be positive, we want to build and the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe who just concluded his speech said nothing worthwhile, Mr. Speaker. All he was able to say was that there are unemployed workers in Lauzon. If anyone knows, I do, and I studied the causes of it. We looked at those causes, we made studies and we drew conclusions and that is why on this side of the House, even if I sit on the government side, I can speak in Ottawa and especially in the province of Quebec.

Steps must immediately be taken to allow the shipbuilding industry in Canada to take its place in the field of international competition so Canada will be recognized as a shipbuilding country. The international situation with respect to shipbuilding is now characterized by six major factors-production costs of Japanese shipbuilding yards; the threat of overproduction hanging over shipbuilding yards throughout the world; financial, administrative and technological changes taking place in European shipbuilding yards; the prospects of the freight market and maritime construction; flags of convenience and competition among different national flags and, finally, the U.S. maritime construction and navigation program.
It is here also that the merchant marine problem merges with the shipyard issue. As a matter of fact, the establishment of a merchant marine would contribute to stabilizing employment in the shipbuilding industry. Let Canada put an end to the agreements concerning the merchant marine which favour ships registered within the Commonwealth and allow them to operate in the Atlantic area. The Canadian government should also make sure that the Arctic waters are national waters that should come under the national coastal trade. The Canadian government should also provide for at least a 50 per cent Canadian content in our international maritime exchanges with the United States and the rest of the world.
Lastly, as I have often mentioned in this House, let the Canadian government limit registration of merchant ships flying the Canadian flag to those built in our national shipyards. We could also establish a shipbuilding research centre whose cost would be shared by concerns and various levels of government, and create an organization to provide communications and facilitate exchanges between governments, ship owners and shipyards.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe agrees with me. And I still find it strange that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe should have devoted 90 per cent of his remarks to repeat the contents of the speech and to conclude that it did not mean anything. But I say there is something in the Speech from the Throne. I fully endorse the entire Speech from the Throne, but I can be positive and make suggestions to the government. That is what I would have liked to hear from the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe but that is not what he said. Mr. Speaker, I have heard 22 speeches from Progressive Conservative members and I have not found anything positive in them. We are being told: Our problem is inflation. We know that the problem exists, but the opposition members do not seem to know how to solve it. I have here a newspaper article which says and I quote: "The government did nothing". The article appeared in Le Soleil. I shall talk about it later, if the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe has enough patience to let me finish. I shall come back to the article in about five minutes. Anyway, he can read my comments tomorrow.
Finally, I should like to deal very briefly with a matter' which is very much with us: the oil situation. The energy crisis has certainly had important effects on the industrial sector. Its impact, present as well as future, has not been and will not be consistent however, because we must bear in mind the fact that some industries need much more
March 6, 1974

energy than others. Among these, let us mention the pulp and paper industry, the petrochemical industry, metallurgy, the processing industry for some non-metallie minerals and the food processing industry, all of which are important in Quebec.
It is to be hoped that industries will not suffer too much from the shortage of oil in the next few months. I can assure you that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will keep a very close watch on the international situation and its impact on Canadian industry. Although supply does not seem to be too much of a problem at this time, the problem of prices is not an easy one to solve. Several companies have already made their difficulties known in that area and as stated in the agreement passed following the Federal-Provincial Energy Conference, a price freeze was decided with grants for the Eastern part of the country. The Federal government is now implementing that plan.
Members of the Opposition talk about the oil crisis. It was said on several occasions that there was an oil problem. Some say they want such and such a route for the pipeline, they want it from Sarnia, they want it through the North, they want this or that. It seems that members of the Opposition and especially Progressive Conservatives when they are from the province of Quebec, support a solution which would favor Quebec in the shortest delay with respect to supply but when they are in Northern Ontario, when they are in Toronto, they are in favour of another solution. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is playing politics with a problem as crucial as the one we are faced with. In spite of the short term squabbles, we must realize that we have, on a long term basis, a unique occasion to develop our industrial sectors involved in energy because few countries will be able to guarantee those industries a steady supply. Of course, if those resources are to attrack industry they must be available at competitive prices.
Mr. Speaker, in the last session I was pleased to see several pieces of legislation passed which dealt with subjects I had included in my speech on the budget on February 21, 1973. On other points, I see that substantial progress was made towards future legislation.
However, there are two suggestions which I then made and would like to discuss in the House in the near future. I draw them again to your attention. The first deals with housing. In my opinion, it would be advisable that the government considers granting an income tax deduction on the construction of family dwellings, in order to encourage Canadians to become home owners.
Since the owners of public and commercial buildings are allowed each year a certain depreciation on their properties, it would seem logical that the owners of family dwellings be entitled to the same privileges as well as an income tax deduction on maintenance costs and other expenditures incurred, such as interest on mortgages. They could also be claimed as a tax deduction. Such measures would stimulate the construction industry while attaining the aim of the government which is that a great number of families become owners of their home.
Another suggestion which I also made dealt with the CNR employees. They have indeed obtained a retroactive 2 per cent salary raise, but this is not their only demand.
The Address-Mr. R. Guay
They wish to obtain pension fund parity with Air Canada employees and civil servants.
Presently, CN employees wonder why, being employees of a Crown Corporation, they do not get exactly the same treatment as other employees of corporations which fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
I know perfectly well that an hon. member on this side of the House is about to introduce a Bill on that matter and I wish to emphasize that I will be pleased to support it.
To conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few personal comments about the Local Initiative Program. I realize that in the Estimates for the fiscal year 1973-74, the LIP budget has been further reduced. This decision being unjustified, in my view, I wish to make two proposals to this House. Either we should completely abolish this program which in its present state causes but dissatisfactions and disappointments among the people, or we should discuss in committee a proper way of applying this program in a more efficient way.
I was pointing out a few things a moment ago, before the departure of the Hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. I do not know whether he is going to the province of Quebec while his leader is here but I know that whenever his leader, the hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), is in Quebec, he in turn is here. Last Sunday, there was a benefit cocktail in Quebec City for Progressive Conservative partisans and this is related to my remarks, since it emphasizes first the absence of the Hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, and then that of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). In every speech, we have been told that the dear child of Joliette was back home. He was going along with the Leader at that time. Well, I want to ask the Leader if, in Quebec, at the present time, it is one thing to find the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle), and another thing to loose the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe and the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi?
When the leader of the opposition was visiting his supporters-who, by the way, are not that many in Quebec- two thirds of his members in Ottawa were absent. Fortunately, the hon. member for Joliette has come back to the fold, because the whole caucus would have been absent.
I find it very amusing that this member should make his first official trip with his leader in Quebec when he himself, on every TV and radio network, following caucus meetings on topics of particular interest to Quebec, makes statements to the media repeating what Mr. Balcer once said in the House: There is no room for a Quebec French Canadian in the Progressive Conservative party.
How can he, this is the question the hon. member for St-Hyacinthe was asking a moment ago, explain in the ridings of Joliette or Saint-Hyacinthe the inaction of government? Personally, in Joliette, I would have simply asked the member for that riding to explain his change of heart. For that matter, he follows in the footsteps of his Quebec leader who has had many changes of heart.
I have here, an item that appeared in Monday's issue of the newspaper Le Soleil. The article was entitled as follows:

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. R. Guay
Robert Lome Stanfield rewrites Quebec's history
The article reads as follows:
Saturday night, Robert Lome Stanfield encouraged the Quebec conservatives to write a new chapter in the province's history, a chapter entitled: "The province reconquered".
Of all the Quebec members sitting in this House, none, I think, who is really aware of what happened in Quebec in the years 1760 during the conquest would have dared say that in Quebec. It is the Conservative leader who comes to conquer us again, under the "tory" banner, a party made up of Englishmen.
Don't take the Quebec people for fools. We were conquered once, more than 200 hundred years ago, and it still hurts. I shall not tolerate any attempt to reconquer us in 1974. Perhaps the leader of the official opposition meant his conquest of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). It could be that I say that anyone trying to reconquer the province of Quebec and banking on the hon. member for Joliette will have a lot of work to do. The way he keeps changing his mind, the hon. member could very well be in another political party at the time of the next election.
I note something else in that article on the great speech on the leader of the official opposition. I ask the members of the opposition to pay close attention to what I am about to quote: The Trudeau government "has done nothing" to check inflation, the Liberal government "has done nothing" to solve the oil crisis, the Liberal government "has done nothing, absolutely nothing". But, in the same speech, he contradicts himself, and I quote the words the leader of the official opposition spoke in Quebec:
Since January 4, 1973, we have seen the Liberal government adopt, one after the other, quite a few of our policies and ideas, which it had previously spurned, derided.
Does that mean that when the government accepts the positive suggestions of the opposition, when they are positive, when they can be passed by the House, it does "nothing"? Some inconsistency! I put the question to the leader of the official opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I say that this speech is a mass of inconsistencies. They say that we have "done nothing". And yet, we have done everything the Progressive Conservatives had recommended we should do. Which means that they did not recommend much and they did not do anything for Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, I am almost through with my remarks. When they talk about "conquest" of when they say:
"La Belle Province should keep in mind that the Conservative Party was the only one to stand up for Quebec with respect to oil supplies and prices.
But I simply ask what steps they proposed as a solution to this problem, to "resoudre a l'avantage", as the leader of the opposition says when he comes to Quebec, what single measure, if any, have they proposed, except to say: The government is powerless, the government "has done nothing".
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I dare hope that before the end of the throne speech debate, at least one Conservative in the House will have a concrete proposal to make. If the Con-

servatives did not understand my French, I ask them to read it in French tomorrow in Hansard. I have made proposals to the government and I know it is willing to listen to us. But the opposition can only criticize, so they are beyond help-
