You read it tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, people come to Quebec and say: "Let La Belle Province remember ... " Quebec remembers one thing especially, and that is the Conservative members of Parliament. The same article refers also to the official language. What did the Progressive Conservatives and the Social Crediters do about this? They separated and said: We are still hesitant. Out west, the members of Parliament said: Understand that we have protected you. Then, in Quebec they said something else. A few Quebec members voted for the bill on official languages. As for the Social Crediters, what did they do? When the vote was taken on the official languages bill they abstained from voting. They said: "It is not enough!" When one says it is not enough, when one refuses to make the first move, how can one march in step. If nobody makes the first move, things come to a standstill. I blame them severely and the Quebec people will also blame them for taking this attitude.
Mr. Speaker, we have heard about a solution: The Leader of the Official Opposition goes around the country saying: Well, we will freeze prices for 90 days and after that, we will see, we will look into the matter, we will set up committees and then see how to deal later with the problem of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, everyone can see that these people are irresponsible, and I think the public, the Canadian people, cannot trust a party that has never proposed a policy which would benefit not only Westerners or Quebecers, but all Canadians.
The Liberal party, with our prime minister, was not afraid to go out West during the federal-provincial conference of western prime ministers to discuss problems and put forward solutions for the benefit of the western people. It was not afraid to come to Quebec to face problems, because only the Liberal party is and will remain the party of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my comments on the Speech from the Throne, I should like to refer briefly to the words used by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. May I say that when I hear a speech like his I am extremely embarrassed. It hurts me to see a grown man representing a riding as large as his stand in this House and cry. All he says, in essence, is: Give us an indication of your policies. This is what we have heard over and over again. They want us to govern, but they want to be the government.
March 6, 1974

Like other members of parliament I had the privilege of listening to the speech from the Throne and hearing what was said by the mover and seconder of the Address, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by various cabinet ministers as well as by supporters of the government. I believe the people of Canada will be as disappointed as I am by the contents of the Speech from the Throne. We are living in troubled times here in Canada. We are in difficulty economically. We are not sure what the future will bring. The country is looking desperately for leadership. It has occurred to many, as it has occurred to me, that all we hear in the Speech from the Throne is, really, a rehashing of policies which have been in Liberal speeches from the throne for the last 15 years.
I should like to deal with some of the deficiencies in the Speech from the Throne, deficiencies which affect small businesses, defiencies which affect the labouring people of the nation, deficiencies which affect the housewife, the merchant, those who are trying desperately to get along on fixed incomes. However, I have been delegated to deal with the Speech from the Throne as it concerns agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I have known the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for a great many years, even before we both became members of this House. He is a man for whom I have a great deal of respect and affection. I have a great deal of affection for him as an individual. But I consider that his response, as minister, to the needs of the industry and of the nation, to be less than effective. He has travelled across the breadth of this nation making, perhaps, more speeches than any other Minister of Agriculture in our nation's history. He has assured the nation that the farmers of Canada are second to none in productivity. He is correct. He has assured the farmers that they are tops in efficiency. He is correct in that too. The Minister of Agriculture has told the farm community that they are second to none in the world. That, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely true, because if they had lacked those qualifications none of them could have survivied the last six years of Liberal administration as far as agriculture is concerned.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let us recall one of the speeches the minister made. It was at the Outloook Conference. This throws light on the manner in which he is carrying out his responsibilities. He said:
We are watching energy supplies. We are watching fertilizer supplies. We are watching equipment supplies. We are watching steel production. We are watching agricultural chemicals. We are watching agriculture stocks and we are watching international markets.
Mr. Speaker, the minister and the other members of the present government are probably the greatest Canadian spectators of all time. But what the farmers want is not conversation or spectator entertainment; they want to know when the minister will get off his podium, sit at the drafting thble and begin to introduce legislation so that some of his fantasies could become facts.
In his speech the other day-and I was amused by this- the minister said:
X note that an hon. member suggests that this is a Conservative policy-
The Address-Mr. Danforth
The reference was to the program for agriculture which the minister had just outlined and which had been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. He said:
I note that an hon. member suggests that this is a Conservative policy. I note he has been reading some of my speeches and is adopting some of my ideas.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He was right. The minister stole them from us.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We need only go back to the 1958 policies of the Conservative party. There one would find, almost verbatim, the proposed 1974 policy of the government, with one small exception, that is, the reference to payment for grain storage in eastern Canada. It is no wonder members of the Conservative party recognize these proposals. They, themselves, were the proponents and authors of that policy. Now, we see it incorporated in Liberal policy for 1974. Mr. Speaker, the policy was good in the 'sixties but surely it is not adequate for the 'seventies.
We have entered a new era. There is a revolution in agriculture. There is a brand new ball game, and some new rules are required.
If agriculture is to make progress, a long-range policy is needed. The policies proposed must be credible. There must be confidence in the minister and in the government. But they have done everything possible to discredit the minister and discredit themselves. I should just like to give a few illustrations of what I mean. One of the greatest concerns of the primary producers of Canada today is the availability of fertilizer and its price. I should like to quote what the Minister of Agriculture said to the growers of this nation, as reported at page 1248 of Hansard for February 13, 1973:
Having done some research and made telephone calls, I wish to report... that the price of fertilizer will not increase.
The price of fertilizer has almost doubled, Mr. Speaker. The minister also said that we must be thankful we have the farmers we have in Canada. After the crass Liberal policies we have had, we surely can be thankful that we have any farmers at all left in Canada.
The minister also said that we must be very cautious that we do not do something that would discourage them. I should like to deal with some of the actions this government has taken which are discouraging farmers, and I do not have to look very far. I should like to deal with the beef industry, the representatives of which are in Ottawa today. The price at which this industry is being asked to sell its products is less than cost of production. Beef producers in this country today are losing thousands and thousands of dollars. As a matter of fact, many of them have already gone bankrupt. Many more are contemplating bankruptcy, and havoc will be created so far as future production of beef is concerned unless the government does something to correct the situation, and does it now.
I should like to repeat what the minister said about this, not today but at a prior meeting with the cattle producers. He said:
During my discussions with the cattlemen's associations and others I found them to be as happy a group of producers as I have found in any part of our nation.

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. Danforth
How ironic it is that the producers who are his friends, and who are so happy, are the very ones who are going bankrupt at the present time as a result of the policies of this government. And the minister says that we must be very cautious that we do not do something that would discourage them! The minister scares me to death when he talks like this.
I want to deal with another commodity about which he has made a statement. The minister has said that more stability has been provided to the dairy industry than any other sector of the agriculture industry in Canada. I ask, what stability? We have the same dairy production in Canada today as we had 100 years ago. It cannot provide for the needs of the Canadian people today, when three or four years ago it was producing an abundance of butter and milk powder for export, with hundreds of thousands of pounds in storage. There were adequate supplies of cheese, butter and milk powder for all Canadian citizens at a reasonable price. Yet the government says it has provided stability. What has the government done in its search for stability? One thing it did was to establish quotas and to say that anyone under a certain quota-and the government set the minimum-would get no subsidy or support. What did this do, Mr. Speaker? It put every little milk and cream producer out of business.
Then, the government was not satisfied with that. It said that what it would do with the quotas was to fix it so that anyone who went over quota would be fined $1.25 per one hundred pounds of milk produced over quota. What has been the result of this? Dairy production in Canada has degenerated to such an extent that this year we are going to have to import 54 million pounds of butter to supply our own domestic needs. No wonder the minister says that we have to turn the dairy industry right around. I wonder what he means by that, because he has already turned it upside down. This is why we are so anxious about government policy and want to know what is going on.
We are also very concerned about the poultry industry. The minister has stated there must be more and more production to fight the increase in inflation. Yet this is the same government that slaughtered two million head of poultry in this country. We had too much poultry and now we are told we do not have enough. The government says we must put emphasis on the production of food and that we must have more food. The farmers must take acres out of fallow and provide more food for the nation and for export. And this is the very government that paid farmers not to grow wheat. The government now says they must grow wheat and it is doing everything it can to get them to grow wheat. This is the type of stability we have, Mr. Speaker, and it is why it is a mockery for the government to say that we have to be very cautious that we do not do something to discourage agriculture.
I should like to say a few words about sugar, something very dear to me. The government has said that we must have a sugar policy and do something about the price of sugar. The government and this Minister of Agriculture were the very ones who put the sugar beet growers in Ontario completely out of business. Now, the minister says we have to establish a sugar industry in southwestern Ontario, the very industry that it put out of business. The

government stopped the subsidy of $700,000 to Ontario producers to produce sugar beets in an endeavour to save money. It then paid the same farmers $1.5 million to stay out of the sugar beet industry. Today, the minister says that we must establish a new industry, that it may cost $30 million to build a new plant. How has this government established any credibility? How can we believe the government is sincere when it tells us its programs are designed to help the farmers?
If anyone had any doubt about the sincerity of this government, let them read the Speech from the Throne. According to the Speech from the Throne, it is government policy to provide high quality food to Canadian consumers at lower prices. Then, the government turns round and says that we have to encourage the farmers of this nation to grow more food at a greater return to the farmers. Anyone who knows anything about business should know that you cannot have cheaper food and pay the farmers more. That is no policy at all. It is not possible, practical, feasible or credible. This is why the government is in trouble.
What has the government done to the beef producers of this country? First of all, it placed an embargo on beef shipments to the United States, our traditional market. Then, it lifted that embargo. Then, it took off the tariff protection we had against imports of U.S. beef flooding our market. Then that was not good enough; the government put it back on again and doubled the tariff. Then, it reduced the tariff gradually to its original floor. Now, when our industry is being crippled as never before, the government is considering what else it can do. When the government comes up with some plan I just do not know whether it will help or hinder. I shudder every time the Minister of Agriculture makes some proposal or puts forward some new policy. We are told not to interfere, to be very cautious about doing anything. Yet the government has changed its policy on beef alone six times in six months. How can agriculture thrive with a policy like that, Mr. Speaker?
We in the vegetable industry in Canada depend for the most part on tariff protection in order to survive. If there is one thing we must have in Canada today it is a guaranteed, stable production of fruits and vegetables. Who would ever believe that the housewives of this country would go to the grocery stores and find the shelves bare of fruits or vegetables either in the fresh, frozen or processed form; but that is what is happening. It is happening because this government kept tinkering with tariffs and reducing them so that many of our vital industries have gone out of business. In my area there used to be thousands of acres devoted to the production of early fruits and vegetables. However, these producers have found that under the reduced tariff protection offered by this government they could not continue in business.
What happened? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in this House a few weeks ago, without consultation with any segment of the agricultural industry and perhaps not even with the Minister of Agriculture, eliminated the tariff on many fruits and vegetables coming into this country. Immediately there was chaos in the Canadian industry because this was done at a time when production
March 6, 1974

was coming in. Many of our markets collapsed as a result of this action by the government. The actions of this government where the farmers and agriculture are concerned are those of an antiquated body which either does not understand at all the complex agricultural industry or does not give a damn about the farmers. It is one or the other. There is no other explanation for these policies that have been carried out.
I should like to speak of another problem in respect of agriculture. We must have some policy in this regard because we are in trouble. It deals with farm labour in southwestern Ontario in the harvest and planting seasons. There is difficulty obtaining labour. The government establishes minimum wages. We have tried to compete, but the result is that there are not sufficient people to do the work there. We have attempted in every way possible to encourage people to come from other parts of Canada and even offshore. What does the government do? It sends a group of people down to that area to inspect the working conditions of the labourers who go there. They find a single case of abuse in respect of housing, at least an alleged abuse. On the basis of that, the publicity goes out across this nation that the employers in that area abuse their privileges as employers and make the position of the employees almost untenable. There is reference to substandard wages paid by the growers in that area. The wages paid in that area are comparable to those paid by the automobile factories adjacent to them. If they were not, there would not be any labourers available.
The very objectives of this government, without investigation of the facts and without listening to the representations of the agricultural groups, have made it almost impossible for us to have enough labourers to take off our crops. Excursions were started into the area by this government. These excursions involved young people from all over the nation with a view to helping us with this problem. "Excursion" is the word for it because these young people came at government expense. They got off the buses, the planes, the taxis and the trains, looked around, said it was a good district, and then got back on the planes, trains and buses and said to the government "Thank you for the trip". There were some exceptions involving young people who worked for an hour or three hours in order to see what it was like, so that they could go back to school and write an essay about how they worked in the fields. Now, the government is talking about a pool of labour from which the employers can obtain labour to help them. This is not regular labour. They have to take their chance and they can do this provided there is adequate government inspection of the working premises in order to determine that conditions are acceptable, not to the workers, but to the government inspectors.
This is the reason the agricultural community lacks faith in this government. This is the reason the agricultural community lacks faith in the Minister of Agriculture. They like him as a person. I like him as a person, but unless he can produce some effective policies he will be completely discredited, not only across this nation and in this House but in his own riding. That would be unfortunate indeed, because I think without a doubt he is the only individual on that side of the House who knows anything at all about farming. Perhaps he is the only practising farmer on the government benches today. Perhaps that is
The Address-Mr. Danforth
the reason we are in trouble; I do not know. I had great hopes when he was appointed Minister of Agriculture. I am from a neighbouring riding of his and I had great hopes. I went to him and told him that I would do everything in my power to help him in his programs to help the farmers. However, it became evident that, although he had some ideas, he was unable to convince his colleagues. Had he had any influence over his colleague the Minister of Finance, perhaps we would not have had the reduction of the tariff on foodstuffs.
In the Speech from the Throne there is a suggestion that the government intends to do great things in respect of transportation. There is no mention of transportation as it relates to agriculture. When we talk about transportation in the House everyone in Canada thinks there will not be sufficient boxcars to move the grain to the coast. But that is only one part of the problem. The housewives of this country are becoming very concerned over the fact that there are not sufficient canned goods on the shelves when they go to the grocery stores. The shelves are becoming more and more bare. It is true that in some cases the fruits and vegetables are available in the warehouses of the companies which manufacture them, but there are absolutely no cars available to transport these goods to the retail stores. There are no boxcars. I spoke to the manager of a canning plant in southwestern Ontario who said that so far as he was concerned-and this is just one of many instances-they are 140 boxcars behind last year's minimum effort in respect of shipping goods. He said they are attempting by all possible ways to get the goods on the market. They are paying premium transportation rates for trucks and every sort of licensed vehicle they can obtain with the result that the consumer will have to pay more money for these goods. I do not want to hear the government blame producers for the high cost.
Much of the blame for the increased cost of food today can be laid at the doorstep of this government. Is it not ridiculous to think that we have a Minister of Agriculture going around this country saying that so far as the producers are concerned the price of food is still not high enough and that the farmers should have more for their produce, then have another minister saying they will do everything they can to drive down the prices of food. I am speaking of course of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray). That is in direct opposition to the Minister of Agriculture. Then, we have the third minister in this unholy triumvirate so far as agriculture is concerned, the Minister of Finance, who wants cheaper food not because of concern for the consumer but because of political expediency and the fantastic dream that the importation of cheap food will force down the cost of living.
This government's policy is not formulated for the farmers of this nation. I might use the old cliche that is so true in respect of agriculture. The government staggers from crisis to crisis. It has taken the Conservative policy of 1958, has constantly revamped and patched it and reproposed it to the present date. I am not surprised at hon. members over there asking us what we would do, because it is evident that in all departments they are bereft of ideas. I am as convinced as my colleagues that when the people are again asked to give a mandate they will vote for a party which is progressive, which shows

March 6, 1974
The Address-Mr. Poulin
some initiative and has some policies to solve crises. Over and over again I have sat in my seat listening to the members of the government condemn us for even proposing price, wage and income control, yet all they have to do is look at the results of their own monetary and fiscal policies to see that they have been an absolute disaster. They must devise other ways of tackling these problems. Perhaps we do not know all the answers but we are not wrong all the time.
This nation must have a policy that will lift us out of the doldrums in which we find ourselves today in order that we can again become a nation among nations. We have a golden opportunity to be a leader among nations, but we cannot hope to be under this present government's policies. This government says it cannot take action because our problems are worldwide. I suggest that under a progressive government we would once again become a leader instead of a follower.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first add my congratulations to those of my colleagues who have already spoken in this debate to the mover (Mr. Stollery) and the seconder (Mr. Pelletier (Sherbrooke)) of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I wish every one of the constituents of the hon. members for Spadina and Sherbrooke could have been here to hear those speeches. Had that been possible, I am sure those hon. members would win their ridings in the next election by landslides. In any case, they certainly did justice to their cause and deserve to be proud, as we are proud of their outstanding contributions to this debate.
May I also extend my warm regards to His Excellency and Madame Leger, with the wish that their term in office provide them with much happiness and peace. I can see already that they will make a great contribution to Canada.
Having said that, may I also welcome all of you, my colleagues, back to my riding, as the parliament buildings are, of course, part of Ottawa Centre, the riding I have the honour to represent. This afternoon I have heard those opposite say they are having some difficulties dealing with government. May I also offer to those who live within my riding, as many here do, the services of my constituency office at 340 Elgin Street to help with any problems they may have.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Give us a new member of parliament.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You would then be busy 24 hours a day.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am already busy 24 hours a day. Ottawa Centre is the heart of the national capital area, not only politically but culturally and socially as well. It is for this reason I have spoken on a number of occasions of my conviction that the National Gallery of Canada, presently in quarters that were never intended to be more than temporary, remain in its present general area. To be more specific, I should like to see the new National Gallery built on the land directly south of the National Arts Centre, and

the land of Cartier Square, which is presently occupied by a temporary Department of National Defence building, become a parkland area for the citizens of the area known locally as Centretown as well as for the citizens of the nation who come here to visit.
Ottawa Centre, as the political heart of the nation's capital, also finds a majority of the 125,000 federal public servants in the national capital area working within it. Many of these people also live within the riding. Bilingualism in the public service is thus a matter of concern. However, I know that the vast majority of public servants accept and endorse, as do I, the policy of bilingualism as stated in the legislation passed by this House in June of last year. The concern which has been expressed in the past over the implementation of the Official Languages Act among public servants has decreased substantially in past months. A couple of weeks ago there was a new flutter of concern about bilingualism when it was reported that the number of positions to be classified bilingual would probably be greater than the original estimate, but surely this issue of numbers is not a real one to any reasonable minded Canadian.
Recently the Ottawa Journal hit the nail on the head. In its lead editorial on Wednesday, February 20, regarding bilingual positions under the heading "Its Need-Not Numbers" it stated:
The purpose of designating bilingual positions is to give effect to the will of parliament, to assure the right of all Canadians to communicate with their federal government in the language of their choice, to ensure the right of public servants to work for the federal government in either official language.
Therefore, whether the number of bilingual public service positions is 25,000 or closer to 50,000 is not an issue.
In addition, as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) has stated, the principal reason for not disclosing the total or an approximate number of bilingual positions stems from the firm commitment of this government to the staff associations that they would be consulted and fully advised before any official disclosure or determination was made.
Last year $2 million was applied toward the stimulation of bilingual education in the lower grade schools in this community. These federal funds were spread out among the four area school boards in the national capital area on the Ottawa side. May I say from personal experience that this has been of great benefit to all of the children who had the opportunity through this federal funding to learn a second official language. It should be continued and I would urge the government and the President of the Treasury Board to consider very seriously making the same amount of money, or more if necessary, available in order to encourage the learning of the official languages in our schools in the national area.
However, the official languages policy is only one area in which there is a two way relationship between the employer, the government, and the employee, the public servant. Salaries represent another such area, and here also the government must act as a responsible employer, and the public servant must act as a responsible employee. Salary increases must keep up with the increase in the cost of living, but at the same time they must be such as not to add to the inflationary pressures in this country.
March 6, 1974

Ottawa Centre, however, in many ways is not unique among urban ridings. This riding has many of the same social and economic problems that are present in numerous other urban ridings. However, in the case of Ottawa Centre, the federal government has special responsibilities as the federal government itself is a major landowner, tenant and employer. For this and many other apparent reasons I again urge the government, as it has been urged many times in past parliaments, to establish a joint parliamentary committee to study the present and future development of the national capital and the national capital area, a committee composed of members of this House and of the Senate, of members from all parts of Canada. It is my determined belief that not only are we blessed by Providence with the finest country in the word but also blessed with potentially having the finest national capital in the world as well.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Take Lebreton flats for example. This is a choice area of land, formerly partly residential, on the shore of the Ottawa River just to the west of the parliament buildings. As a matter of fact this vacant area of land can be seen from the parliamentary restaurant. This land was acquired by the federal government in 1961, and has lain idle since that time. When the land was first acquired, the plan was to use it as the site for the new National Defence Headquarters. That plan did not materialize. In the mid-1960's much of the land was earmarked for arterial road construction. Fortunately, nothing came of that plan.
Again, I urge that work begin immediately on a concept plan for Lebreton Flats. It is my recommendation that this area be developed for housing so that the people of Canada will be able to use and enjoy this choice area of the national capital. Because of its proximity to downtown Ottawa this land is too valuable to lie idle. I envisage an integrated, forward-looking community for this area, a community of various types of housing to accommodate a cross-section of Canadian society, a community which has its educational and commercial requirements taken into consideration from the beginning, an area which would lend itself also to exemplary recreational facilities for Canadians of all ages and interests including, for example, much needed soccer fields for this sport which is rapidly becoming so popular. There have been encouraging signs in recent months for this type of proposal. I urge the National Capital Commission that, starting immediately, it report monthly progress on development of a concept plan for Lebreton flats along the lines that I have suggested.
To be taken into consideration when developing Lebreton flats should be the citizens in the area directly to the south, that is, Dalhousie Ward. The residents of Dalhousie Ward have published a study, done almost exclusively by the people of the area but financed by a $45,000 federal
The Address-Mr. Poulin
government grant from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The initiative of the residents of Dalhousie Ward, of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and of the minister responsible for it, all deserve a great deal of credit for this experiment in urban planning.
As the minister mentioned earlier in his remarks today, an agreement has been reached between the province and the federal government with respect to the neighbourhood improvement program and with respect to the residential improvement program. The plan, as I say, was developed by the residents of Dalhousie Ward. It is now being considered by the citizens of the ward. It will then go to the municipal officials, and I would only state to the people of that area, to the minister, to the municipal officials, and to the corporation that they will have my entire support in having that area designated in order that it qualify for the neighbourhood and residential improvement programs as enacted by recent legislation.
I now wish to turn to some national issues, Mr. Speaker, It was heartening to me, and to most Canadians, to see mention in the Speech from the Throne of such a wide range of measures to impede inflation, and especially inflation in the area of food prices. I note particularly the measures that will result in increasing the supply of food, for this is the only long-term solution to the complex problem of increasing food prices. Here I mention measures such as assistance to farmers to help them modernize their methods, assistance to young farmers to help them get established in agriculture, improvements to marketing systems, and the availability of manpower, especially during peak periods.
I note the twin commitments in the throne speech that on the one hand the producer must be assured a fair income for his work, and on the other hand that the consumer must be ensured a fair value for his dollar. I quote from the speech:
He must be protected against disruptive increases in the price of essential food stuffs caused by international market demand. Guarantees against unduly low prices to producers must be coupled with guarantees against unduly high prices to consumers.
In the past several days we have heard that bread prices are likely to rise in the near future. However the fact remains that without Liberal government action last summer and fall, bread prices today would be 10 or 12 cents more per loaf than they are now.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is two minutes to six o'clock, and I wonder if at this time I could call it six o'clock as I am just about to go to another topic.
